questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 2 month history of a tight ache in her jaw and left arm when she walks briskly to work on cold mornings. It goes within 3 minutes of stopping. She smokes and has hypercholesterolaemia. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. Her resting ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Constricting pain in the jaw or arm brought on by exertion (worse in cold) and relieved by rest within minutes, in a smoker with high cholesterol, is stable angina.

clues: tight ache in her jaw and left arm
steps.x: Constricting pain **in the jaw/arm**, on **exertion**, relieved by **rest**, with vascular risk factors.

elim: Jaw pain would be constant and not brought on by exertion.
Related to meals and lying flat, not exertion, and not relieved by rest.
Reproducible on palpation or movement, not on walking in the cold.
Needs pain at rest or a worsening pattern; hers is predictable and unchanged.

steps.x: **D. Stable angina.** Angina need not be in the chest: jaw, neck or arm pain on exertion relieved by rest counts.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has a 6 week history of a sharp, stabbing pain in his left chest. It comes on when he climbs stairs and settles within 2 minutes of resting. It does not feel tight or heavy. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. His examination is normal.
questions.q: How should his chest pain be classified?
questions.e: The three features of anginal pain are constricting discomfort, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within minutes. Two of three is atypical angina; all three is typical.

clues: does not feel tight or heavy
steps.x: Exertional (1), relieved by rest (2), but **not constricting**: two of three features.

elim: Needs one or none of the three features; he has two.
Needs all three features; his pain is not constricting.
Pain at rest or a worsening pattern; his is predictable.
Occurs at rest, often at night, from vasospasm.

steps.x: **A. Atypical angina.** 3 features = typical angina; 2 = atypical; 0 to 1 = non-anginal.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a 2 month history of central chest heaviness spreading to his neck when he mows the lawn. It eases within 5 minutes of using his GTN spray or sitting down. It has not changed in pattern and he has never had pain at rest. He has a strong family history of heart disease.
questions.q: How should his chest pain be classified?
questions.e: Constricting pain in the chest or neck, brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or GTN within minutes, has all three features of typical angina.

clues: central chest heaviness spreading to his neck
eases within 5 minutes of using his GTN spray
steps.x: Constricting + exertional + relieved by rest/GTN = **all three** features.

elim: Only two of the three features; he has all three.
One or none of the features.
Vasospastic pain at rest, not exertional.
He has no rest pain and no change in pattern.

steps.x: **D. Typical angina.** All three features = typical angina; stable pattern = stable angina.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has had two episodes of central chest tightness at rest today, each lasting 15 minutes. She is now pain free. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. Her ECG shows no ST elevation. High-sensitivity troponin at arrival and 3 hours (see item resources) is within the reference range.

visual.title: High-sensitivity troponin
visual.caption: Flat and below the upper limit of 14 ng/L: no myocardial necrosis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ischaemic chest pain at rest with a normal troponin is unstable angina (plaque rupture without infarction); a raised troponin would make it an NSTEMI.

steps.x: Rest pain = ACS, **normal troponin** = no infarction.

elim: Needs a rise in troponin above the reference range.
Pleuritic, positional pain with saddle-shaped ST elevation.
There is no ST elevation.
Stable angina is exertional and predictable, never at rest.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Rest or crescendo pain + normal troponin = unstable angina.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has had stable angina on walking 500 metres for 2 years. Over the last 10 days it has come on after 50 metres and now needs two puffs of GTN to settle. He has not had pain at rest. His ECG is unchanged and two troponins are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A rapidly worsening (crescendo) pattern of angina, even without rest pain, is unstable angina; normal troponins exclude infarction.

steps.x: Pain threshold falling fast = **crescendo**, so no longer stable.

elim: Breathlessness and oedema, not worsening exertional chest pain.
Troponin would be raised.
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness, not crescendo exertional pain.
His pattern has changed; stable angina is predictable and unchanging.

steps.x: **E. Unstable angina.** Worsening angina = unstable angina, even before rest pain appears.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had 25 minutes of central chest pain at rest last night that has now settled. He is pain free and his troponin is normal. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. His ECG (see item resources) is shown.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG, pain free
visual.caption: Deep symmetrical T-wave inversion in V2 and V3.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rest pain that has settled with deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3 is Wellens syndrome, a warning of critical proximal LAD stenosis.

steps.x: Pain-free after **rest pain**, deep T inversion **V2–V3**.

elim: Gives widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression.
Coved ST elevation in V1 and V2, presenting with syncope.
Flattened T waves and U waves in all leads, not deep T inversion in V2–V3.
Tall voltages with lateral (V5–V6) T inversion.

steps.x: **E. Wellens syndrome.** Wellens = deep/biphasic T waves in V2–V3 = critical proximal LAD: needs angiography, not a stress test.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman had chest pain at rest 2 days ago that lasted 20 minutes. She is pain free with a normal troponin. Invasive coronary angiography later shows a 95% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her pain-free ECG before angiography?
o: Q waves in II, III and aVF
Saddle-shaped ST elevation in all leads
ST elevation in II, III and aVF
questions.e: Critical proximal LAD stenosis typically shows Wellens T waves (deeply inverted or biphasic in V2–V3) when the patient is pain free.

steps.x: Proximal LAD lesion found after **rest pain** with normal troponin: Wellens.

elim: Old inferior infarction from the RCA.
Pericarditis.
Lateral ischaemia, not a typical proximal LAD sign.
Acute inferior STEMI, usually RCA.

steps.x: **A. Deep T-wave inversion in V2–V3.** Wellens T waves in V2–V3 point to the proximal LAD.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 3 month history of breathlessness and tiredness when she walks to the shops, relieved within minutes by resting. She has no chest pain. Her Hb, thyroid function and spirometry are normal and her echocardiogram shows normal ventricular and valve function. CT coronary angiography shows a 90% LAD stenosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.e: Elderly diabetic patients often have exertional breathlessness or fatigue instead of pain (an angina equivalent); a significant stenosis with normal echo makes this stable angina.

clues: breathlessness and tiredness when she walks
steps.x: Exertional breathlessness relieved by rest in an **elderly diabetic**, with a stenosis.

elim: Her Hb is normal.
Her spirometry is normal.
Her ventricular function is normal.
Symptoms are predictable and exertional, not at rest or worsening.

steps.x: **D. Stable angina.** Angina can present as breathlessness or fatigue, especially in elderly or diabetic patients.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes and has type 2 diabetes has chest tightness on exertion relieved by rest. There is no murmur and his Hb is 146 g/L. His ECG at rest is normal. CT coronary angiography shows calcified plaques with a 75% stenosis of the right coronary artery.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his chest pain?
questions.e: Ischaemic heart disease is reduced myocardial blood flow from coronary atherosclerosis; the plaque narrows the lumen so flow cannot rise with demand, causing ischaemia and, if it ruptures, infarction.

steps.x: Risk factors + **calcified plaque** + no murmur or anaemia.

elim: His Hb is normal.
Would cause an ejection systolic murmur; none is heard.
Causes pain at rest, not fixed calcified stenoses.
A young person's disease with a murmur and an abnormal ECG.

steps.x: **D. Coronary atherosclerosis.** Angina is almost always coronary atherosclerosis; exclude AS and anaemia.

questions.stem: A 41 year old man has had exertional chest tightness for a month. His father died of a heart attack at 46. He has yellow plaques around his eyelids and thickened, nodular Achilles tendons. His total cholesterol is 9.8 mmol/L. CT coronary angiography shows LAD disease.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying risk factor for his angina?
questions.e: Premature IHD with tendon xanthomata, xanthelasma, very high cholesterol and a family history of early MI is familial hypercholesterolaemia (hyperlipidaemia and family history are major risk factors).

clues: father died of a heart attack at 46
steps.x: Young + **tendon xanthomata** + family history of early MI.

elim: No raised BP is described.
Can raise cholesterol but does not cause tendon xanthomata.
Not mentioned in the history.
No hyperglycaemia is described.

steps.x: **A. Familial hypercholesterolaemia.** Premature angina with tendon xanthomata = familial hypercholesterolaemia.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has had stable angina for 3 years, always after about 15 minutes of walking uphill. Today it came on running for a bus, felt identical, and settled 2 minutes after her GTN spray. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. Her ECG is unchanged from last year.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pain on a predictable level of exertion, identical to usual, quickly relieved by GTN with an unchanged ECG remains stable angina from a fixed stable plaque.

clues: always after about 15 minutes of walking uphill
settled 2 minutes after her GTN spray
steps.x: Same trigger, same pain, quick relief: **predictable** pattern.

elim: Tearing pain to the back with BP differences, not settling on GTN.
Pain usually lasts over 20 minutes at rest with a troponin rise.
Can respond to GTN but is related to swallowing, not exertion.
Her attack was exertional, familiar and quickly relieved.

steps.x: **D. Stable angina.** Predictable exertional pain relieved by rest/GTN = stable angina.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has atypical chest pain. CT coronary angiography shows a 60% stenosis of the circumflex artery of uncertain significance. He has a dobutamine stress echocardiogram. He develops his usual chest tightness at peak stress.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding at peak stress if the stenosis is significant?
o: Global dilatation of all four chambers
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve
questions.e: Functional imaging (stress echo, stress MRI or perfusion scan) shows ischaemia as a new regional wall motion abnormality in the territory of the stenosed artery when demand rises.

steps.x: Functional test asks: does the muscle supplied by this artery stop moving under **stress**?

elim: Suggests dilated cardiomyopathy, not regional ischaemia.
Not caused by stress-induced ischaemia.
A feature of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Endocarditis.

steps.x: **B. New regional wall motion abnormality.** Stress echo/MRI: inducible regional wall motion abnormality = significant ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with exertional chest tightness has a stress cardiac MRI. At rest wall motion is normal. During adenosine stress there is a perfusion defect and hypokinesia confined to the inferior wall. Her ECG at rest is normal.
questions.q: Which coronary artery is most likely stenosed?
o: Posterior descending artery from the circumflex
questions.e: The inferior wall is usually supplied by the right coronary artery, so an inducible inferior defect points to RCA stenosis.

steps.x: Stress-only defect in the **inferior** wall.

elim: Supplies the lateral wall.
Supplies the anterior wall and septum.
Would cause widespread anterior and lateral ischaemia.
Only in left-dominant circulations, a minority.

steps.x: **E. Right coronary artery.** Inferior = RCA; anterior = LAD; lateral = circumflex.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with stable angina takes bisoprolol 5 mg daily. A locum added verapamil last week for ongoing symptoms. He now feels faint. His pulse rate is 34 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg. His rhythm strip is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Lead II rhythm strip
visual.caption: P waves and QRS complexes unrelated: complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.e: Beta-blockers and verapamil must never be combined: both slow AV conduction, causing bradycardia and complete heart block.

steps.x: New **verapamil** on top of a **beta-blocker**, then heart block.

elim: No chest pain is described and the trigger is the new drug.
He does not take digoxin.
No renal impairment or potassium-raising drugs are described.
Develops over months, not one week after a new drug.

steps.x: **B. Bisoprolol combined with verapamil.** Never combine a beta-blocker with verapamil: risk of complete heart block.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has a 2 month history of central chest tightness walking up hills, relieved by rest within 5 minutes. He has hypertension. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. His resting ECG, FBC and lipid profile have been done. He has no pain at rest.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: CT coronary angiography is first-line for suspected stable angina; functional imaging is second-line and invasive angiography third-line.

clues: walking up hills, relieved by rest
steps.x: Suspected **stable** angina: start non-invasive anatomical imaging.

elim: No longer recommended to diagnose stable angina.
The gold standard, but third-line after non-invasive tests.
Only if an acute coronary syndrome is suspected; his pain is exertional.
Second-line functional test if CTCA is non-diagnostic.

steps.x: **A. CT coronary angiography.** Stable angina: CTCA first, functional imaging second, invasive angiography third.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has had central chest pressure at rest for 40 minutes with nausea and sweating. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg. Her 12-lead ECG shows no ST elevation. She has been given aspirin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When MI is suspected, the bloods must include troponin; it separates unstable angina (normal) from NSTEMI (raised).

steps.x: Rest pain without ST elevation: **is there infarction?**

elim: Used for stable chest pain, not ongoing pain at rest.
For low-probability PE; this sounds ischaemic.
Dangerous with possible ACS.
A test for stable angina; contraindicated in suspected ACS.

steps.x: **D. High-sensitivity troponin.** Suspected ACS without ST elevation: troponin.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has chest tightness on exertion. CT coronary angiography shows moderate stenoses in two arteries but heavy calcification makes the severity hard to judge. He has severe knee osteoarthritis, so he cannot walk on a treadmill.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat CT coronary angiography in 6 months
questions.e: When CTCA is inconclusive, second-line is non-invasive functional imaging: stress echo, stress cardiac MRI or myocardial perfusion scan, using drug stress if he cannot exercise.

steps.x: CTCA **inconclusive** + cannot exercise = pharmacological **functional** imaging.

elim: He cannot exercise, and it is not recommended for diagnosis.
Third-line, after functional imaging, unless symptoms are refractory.
Delays diagnosis; calcification will not improve.
Shows resting function, not inducible ischaemia.

steps.x: **A. Adenosine stress perfusion cardiac MRI.** CTCA inconclusive: functional imaging (stress echo, MRI or perfusion scan).

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has angina limiting her to 100 metres despite bisoprolol and felodipine. A stress perfusion scan shows a large area of inducible anterior ischaemia. Her cardiologist is considering revascularisation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Invasive coronary angiography is the gold standard, used third-line after non-invasive testing, to define anatomy and plan PCI or CABG.

clues: large area of inducible anterior ischaemia
steps.x: Ischaemia proven + symptoms despite 2 drugs = plan **revascularisation**.

elim: First-line diagnostic test; ischaemia is already proven and treatment now needs planning.
Adds nothing after a positive functional scan.
Ischaemia is already shown.
Images valves and the left atrium, not coronary arteries.

steps.x: **C. Invasive coronary angiography.** Gold standard = invasive angiography, used third-line to plan PCI/CABG.

questions.stem: A medical student is recording a 12-lead ECG on a 60 year old man with angina. She places the first chest electrode and asks the nurse to check its position before continuing with the others.
questions.q: Where should lead V1 be placed?
questions.e: V1 sits in the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin and V2 at the left sternal margin; V4 to V6 are in the 5th space at the mid-clavicular, anterior axillary and mid-axillary lines.

steps.x: V1 and V2 straddle the sternum in the **4th** space; V1 is on the **right**.

elim: This is V2.
This is V5.
This is V6.
This is V4.

steps.x: **B. 4th intercostal space, right sternal margin.** V1 right sternal edge, V2 left sternal edge (4th space).

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with exertional chest pain has a 12-lead ECG. The healthcare assistant has placed V1 and V2 correctly. She places the next electrode in the 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, then puts one more electrode between it and V2.
questions.q: Which lead is placed in the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line?
questions.e: V4 is placed in the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, before V3, which goes midway between V2 and V4.

clues: 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
steps.x: Place **V4** first in the 5th space MCL, then V3 halfway back to V2.

elim: A limb lead, from the left leg electrode combination.
V3 is the one placed midway between V2 and V4.
V5 is in the 5th space at the anterior axillary line.
V6 is in the 5th space at the mid-axillary line.

steps.x: **C. V4.** V4 = 5th ICS MCL; V3 = midway between V2 and V4.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with angina is having an ECG to look for lateral ischaemia. The nurse places V4 in the 5th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, then follows the same horizontal level round to his left side for the last two electrodes.
questions.q: Where should lead V6 be placed?
questions.e: V5 is in the 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line and V6 at the mid-axillary line, level with V4.

steps.x: V4, V5 and V6 all sit on the **5th space**: MCL, anterior axillary, mid-axillary.

elim: This is V2.
This is V5.
This is not a standard 12-lead position.
This is V3.

steps.x: **C. 5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line.** V5 = anterior axillary, V6 = mid-axillary (5th ICS).

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with angina has an ECG. Lead I shows inverted P waves, QRS complexes and T waves, and aVR is upright. The chest leads show normal R-wave progression. A repeat ECG an hour earlier on another machine was normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Left and right leg electrodes swapped
Right and left arm electrodes swapped
V1 and V2 placed one space too high
questions.e: The limb electrodes go on the right arm (RA), left arm (LA), right leg (RL, neutral) and left leg (LL); swapping RA and LA inverts lead I and makes aVR look upright, with normal chest leads.

clues: Lead I shows inverted P waves
chest leads show normal R-wave progression
earlier on another machine was normal
steps.x: Limb leads abnormal, **chest leads normal**, previously normal: an electrode error.

elim: Changes would be in V1–V4; chest leads are normal.
Also causes poor R-wave progression across the chest leads, and the earlier ECG was normal.
RL is the neutral electrode; swapping legs barely changes the ECG.
Would change chest leads only.

steps.x: **D. Right and left arm electrodes swapped.** Inverted lead I with normal chest leads = arm electrodes reversed.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has newly diagnosed stable angina confirmed on CT coronary angiography. He has occasional attacks of chest tightness when walking quickly. He asks what to take during an attack. He does not take sildenafil.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his acute attacks?
questions.e: Acute angina is relieved by sublingual GTN spray or tablet; warn about headache and dizziness, and avoid with PDE-5 inhibitors.

steps.x: Relief of an **attack**, not prevention.

elim: Used for suspected ACS, not routine angina attacks.
A regular preventive drug, too slow for an acute attack.
Long-acting nitrate for prevention, not relief.
A preventive add-on drug.

steps.x: **E. Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate.** Acute attacks: sublingual GTN (headache, dizziness).

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has stable angina confirmed on CT coronary angiography. She has started bisoprolol and a GTN spray, and her symptoms are controlled. Her total cholesterol is 5.8 mmol/L. She has no bleeding history or allergies.
questions.q: Which additional treatment would most improve her prognosis?
questions.e: Aspirin (antiplatelet protection against plaque thrombosis) and a statin (plaque stabilisation and LDL lowering) give prognostic benefit; antianginals only relieve symptoms.

steps.x: Question asks about **prognosis**, not symptoms.

elim: Symptom control only; no mortality benefit.
Symptom control only.
Anticoagulation is not indicated for stable angina.
Dual antiplatelet therapy is for ACS or after stenting.

steps.x: **A. Aspirin and atorvastatin.** Angina: symptoms (GTN, BB/CCB) + prognosis (aspirin + statin).

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has stable angina confirmed on CT coronary angiography. He has attacks most days despite using GTN spray. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. He has no asthma, heart failure or conduction disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug to prevent attacks?
questions.e: First-line symptomatic treatment is a beta-blocker (or a rate-limiting CCB); bisoprolol lowers heart rate and contractility, reducing oxygen demand and lengthening diastolic filling.

clues: no asthma, heart failure or conduction disease
steps.x: First-line **prevention**, no contraindication to beta-blockade.

elim: Long-acting nitrates are add-on, not first-line.
A third-line add-on option.
An add-on for refractory angina.
An add-on for refractory angina.

steps.x: **A. Bisoprolol.** Angina prevention: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB first.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has stable angina controlled on atenolol 50 mg daily, aspirin and atorvastatin. Since starting atenolol he has had erectile dysfunction, which he finds unacceptable. He has no asthma or heart failure and is not on any other heart drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate alternative to atenolol?
questions.e: Beta-blockers can cause sexual dysfunction; the alternative first-line drug is a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem or verapamil (also used when beta-blockers are contraindicated, for example in asthma).

clues: not on any other heart drugs
steps.x: Intolerant of beta-blockers: switch to the **other first-line** class.

elim: Another beta-blocker, likely to cause the same side effect.
Add-on drug, not a first-line replacement.
Add-on for refractory angina.
Add-on for refractory angina.

steps.x: **B. Diltiazem.** First-line options: beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB (diltiazem/verapamil).

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with stable angina and severe asthma takes verapamil 120 mg three times daily, aspirin and atorvastatin. She still has angina twice a week. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. She is not suitable for revascularisation at present.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: When verapamil alone is insufficient and beta-blockers are not possible, add a long-acting nitrate (or nicorandil or ranolazine).

clues: still has angina twice a week
steps.x: On **verapamil**, cannot have a **beta-blocker**: add a different class.

elim: Asthma, and must never be combined with verapamil.
Another rate-limiting CCB; adds to AV block risk.
Should not be combined with verapamil (interaction and bradycardia).
Her severe asthma contraindicates beta-blockers.

steps.x: **C. Add isosorbide mononitrate.** Inadequate on verapamil: add a long-acting nitrate, nicorandil or ranolazine.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with angina takes bisoprolol, amlodipine and isosorbide mononitrate 20 mg at 8am and 8pm. For a month the nitrate seems to have stopped working and his angina has returned. He takes all his tablets reliably.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his nitrate?
o: Double the dose, keeping the same times
questions.e: Continuous nitrate exposure causes tolerance; an asymmetric regimen (e.g. 8am and 2pm) gives a nitrate-free interval overnight.

steps.x: Evenly spaced doses = continuous exposure = **tolerance**.

elim: Removes any nitrate-free interval, making tolerance worse.
Tolerance persists without a nitrate-free period.
It will work again once tolerance is prevented.
Continuous exposure maintains tolerance.

steps.x: **D. Take it at 8am and 2pm.** Nitrate tolerance: asymmetric dosing for a nitrate-free interval.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with refractory angina had a new drug added 3 months ago. He now has a painful ulcer near his anus that is slow to heal. He also reports headaches and facial flushing since the drug was started. His other drugs are bisoprolol, amlodipine, aspirin and atorvastatin.
questions.q: Which drug was most likely started 3 months ago?
questions.e: Nicorandil, a potassium channel activator for refractory angina, causes headache and flushing and characteristically gastrointestinal, including anal, ulceration.

steps.x: Refractory angina add-on + **anal ulceration**.

elim: Causes ankle oedema and flushing, but not anal ulcers.
Causes headache and tolerance, not ulceration.
Causes visual phosphenes and bradycardia.
Causes dizziness and constipation, and can prolong QT.

steps.x: **D. Nicorandil.** Nicorandil: headache, flushing, anal ulceration.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has angina on minimal exertion despite bisoprolol 10 mg and felodipine 10 mg daily. Invasive angiography shows disease suitable for PCI, booked in 6 weeks. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate step while she awaits PCI?
questions.e: Bisoprolol plus felodipine is the optimum combination; while awaiting PCI or CABG a third drug, a long-acting nitrate, can be added.

steps.x: Already on optimal **BB + dihydropyridine CCB**, waiting for PCI.

elim: Not an antianginal drug.
Must never be combined with a beta-blocker.
Would worsen her angina.
Rate-limiting CCB plus beta-blocker risks heart block; her pulse is already 58.

steps.x: **B. Add isosorbide mononitrate.** Awaiting revascularisation on two drugs: add a long-acting nitrate.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man without diabetes has angina limiting his walking despite bisoprolol, felodipine and isosorbide mononitrate. Invasive coronary angiography shows a single, short 90% stenosis of the proximal right coronary artery. The other arteries are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Add nicorandil and review in 6 months
questions.e: Refractory angina needs revascularisation; for a simple single-vessel lesion in a younger non-diabetic patient, PCI with stenting is appropriate.

clues: despite bisoprolol, felodipine and isosorbide mononitrate
steps.x: Refractory + **single-vessel**, young, non-diabetic.

elim: He is already on three drugs and needs revascularisation.
Survival advantage is for over 65s, diabetics or complex 3-vessel disease; he has single-vessel disease.
For end-stage heart failure, not single-vessel angina.
For STEMI without PCI access, not stable angina.

steps.x: **D. Percutaneous coronary intervention.** Simple single-vessel disease: PCI; complex, diabetic or over 65: CABG.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman without diabetes has angina despite three antianginal drugs. Invasive coronary angiography shows complex stenoses in the left anterior descending, circumflex and right coronary arteries. She is otherwise fit for surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Add ranolazine and continue medical therapy
Percutaneous coronary intervention to all three arteries
questions.e: CABG has a survival advantage over PCI in complex three-vessel disease and in patients over 65 (and diabetics).

clues: left anterior descending, circumflex and right coronary arteries
steps.x: Over 65 + **complex 3-vessel** disease.

elim: She is already on three drugs and needs revascularisation.
Used for STEMI, not stable angina.
CABG has a survival advantage in complex 3-vessel disease and in over 65s.
For aortic stenosis.

steps.x: **B. Coronary artery bypass grafting.** CABG beats PCI for survival: over 65, diabetics, complex 3-vessel disease.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with stable angina and type 2 diabetes has a clinic BP of 142/88 mmHg on ramipril and amlodipine. His angina is controlled. He asks what his blood pressure should be. His HbA1c is 54 mmol/mol.
questions.q: Which clinic BP target should be advised?
questions.e: BP targets are below 140/90 mmHg in the general population and 135/85 mmHg in people with diabetes.

steps.x: Angina with **diabetes**: the lower target applies.

elim: Too low as a routine target; risks hypotension.
Not a standard NICE target.
The general population target; a lower target applies in diabetes.
The target for people aged 80 and over.
